None of this is Raven's work, and none of it is covered by Raven's own licence. Each entry keeps the terms
it arrived under.

|---|---|---|---|
| `anime4k/` | [bloc97/Anime4K](https://github.com/bloc97/Anime4K) (PyTorch port of the GLSL kernels) | MIT | [`anime4k/LICENSE`](anime4k/LICENSE) |
| `DearPyGui_Markdown/` | [IvanNazaruk/DearPyGui-Markdown](https://github.com/IvanNazaruk/DearPyGui-Markdown) | MIT | [`DearPyGui_Markdown/LICENSE`](DearPyGui_Markdown/LICENSE) |

| `kokoro_fastapi/` | [remsky/Kokoro-FastAPI](https://github.com/remsky/Kokoro-FastAPI) | Apache-2.0 | [`kokoro_fastapi/LICENSE`](kokoro_fastapi/LICENSE) |

## `IconsFontAwesome6.py`

The one entry with no licence text of its own, because it is a **single generated file kept byte-identical to
upstream** — which is worth preserving, since it can then be diffed against upstream and re-vendored by
straight copy. Its terms are recorded here rather than in a header, so that property survives.

Font Awesome splits its terms three ways: icons as SVG and JS are CC BY 4.0, the web and desktop font files
are SIL OFL 1.1, and *"all non-font and non-icon files"* are MIT. This file holds codepoint constants derived
from `icons.yml`, which is neither a font nor an icon, so the MIT clause applies:

> Copyright (c) 2024 Fonticons, Inc. (https://fontawesome.com)

The generator is under zlib, copyright (c) 2017 Juliette Foucaut and Doug Binks; its terms cover whatever
boilerplate it contributed. The `.ttf` files this addresses are a separate matter and ship under OFL 1.1 —
see [`raven/fonts/LICENSE.md`](../fonts/LICENSE.md).

## Adopted, not merely vendored

Everything here **except** `IconsFontAwesome6.py` has diverged from upstream, deliberately: these are treated
as Raven's to fix and extend rather than as pristine snapshots. `tha3` swaps `no_grad` for `inference_mode`
in the hot paths, `DearPyGui_Markdown` is substantially robustified for background-threaded rendering,
`file_dialog` gained sorting and other extensions, `anime4k` was cleaned up, and `kokoro_fastapi`'s writer
differs from its upstream commit by some 70 lines.

That has a licensing consequence worth stating: Raven-authored code lives inside these directories, and it is
under **their** licences rather than Raven's, because a modification to a work carries the work's terms.
Anyone reasoning about what Raven may be taken under has to read this table, not just the top-level
`LICENSE.md`.

**Where a licence demands more than attribution, divergence is not merely worth documenting but required to
be.** Apache-2.0 section 4(b) obliges modified files to carry a prominent notice that they changed, which
applies to `kokoro_fastapi/streaming_audio_writer.py` and to nothing else here — the MIT entries have no
equivalent clause. Check this before adding an Apache-, MPL- or GPL-family dependency to the tree.

## Why only one file of Kokoro-FastAPI

The streaming audio writer is the part Raven needs; the server it belongs to is not. Two reasons, both from
experience rather than preference:

- **Every server is one more thing the user has to start by hand.** The LLM backend earns that cost, being
  highly technical and not worth reimplementing. Raven-server is part of the constellation. A third one, for
  text-to-speech, does not earn it.
- **The word splitting differed.** Getting phoneme timestamps out of the API produced splits that crashed on
  some well-formed inputs, and lipsync needs the *same* splitting everywhere to line up with the audio.
  Running Kokoro locally makes that consistent by construction. The details are in Raven's git log.

Kokoro itself turned out simple enough to integrate directly, which is what made dropping the server
practical. (As of April 2025 that server also pinned a CPU core at 100% while idle — a non-starter on a
laptop. Whether that still holds is unchecked; it is recorded as the reason for a decision, not as a current
claim about upstream.)

## The provenance pattern to copy

`kokoro_fastapi/streaming_audio_writer.py` has the header the rest of this directory should grow. It names
upstream, the *original path within* upstream, the exact commit it was taken from with its date, and the
licence. The pinned commit is what makes the divergence recoverable at all: without it, "modified from
upstream" is unfalsifiable, and re-vendoring means guessing which changes were ours.
